items.title: B2B Customer Discovery Interview
items.summary: A structured interview script to uncover B2B customer pains, workflows and decision criteria
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Use this prompt before starting a new B2B product initiative or feature to understand the prospect's current workflow, their frustrations, and what a successful solution looks like from their perspective.

## Prompt

You are conducting a B2B customer discovery interview for a product manager. Interview me (playing the role of a potential B2B customer) one section at a time. Ask each question and wait for my answer before moving on. Keep your tone professional and inquisitive.

Section 1: Current Workflow
- Walk me through a typical day or week as it relates to [problem area].
- What tools or systems do you currently use?
- Who else in your organisation is involved in this process?

Section 2: Pain Points
- What frustrates you most about the current approach?
- If you could wave a magic wand, what would change?
- How much time or money is lost because of these frustrations?

Section 3: Decision Criteria
- What would a perfect solution look like for you?
- Who else would need to approve such a solution?
- What factors matter most: price, reliability, integrations, speed of implementation?

Section 4: Prioritisation
- How urgent is this problem on a scale of 1-10?
- What would happen if nothing changed in the next 12 months?

When complete, summarise the key findings in a structured format with: persona overview, pain points ranked by severity, decision criteria, urgency assessment, and recommended next steps.

items.title: B2B Pricing Strategy Workshop
items.summary: Guided framework to define and validate B2B pricing models including tiered, usage-based, and enterprise
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Use this prompt when developing or revising a B2B pricing model. It walks through competitive analysis, value-based pricing, tier definition, and packaging strategy.

## Prompt

Act as a B2B pricing strategist. Guide me through developing a pricing model step by step.

Step 1: Ask about the product — what does it do, who is the target buyer, and what is the primary value metric?

Step 2: Competitive landscape — who are the top 3 competitors and how do they price? What gaps exist?

Step 3: Value drivers — what specific outcomes does the product enable (e.g. time saved, revenue increased, risk reduced)? Quantify each.

Step 4: Tier structure — define 3-4 tiers (e.g. Starter, Growth, Business, Enterprise). For each tier define: target customer size, features included, usage limits, and price point.

Step 5: Packaging decisions — which features are tier-gated versus available across all tiers? What add-ons make sense?

Step 6: Validation plan — how would you test these price points? Suggest a Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger approach.

Provide a final summary with tier table, recommended pricing, and a validation timeline.

items.title: B2B Stakeholder Mapping
items.summary: Identify and map all stakeholders in a B2B buying decision, including champions, influencers, blockers, and economic buyers
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

B2B sales almost never involve a single decision maker. Use this prompt to map the full buying committee for a target account or segment.

## Prompt

Act as a B2B product manager helping me map stakeholders for a target account. Ask me questions one at a time.

Start by asking about the target organisation: industry, size, and the department we're selling into.

Then ask me to identify people filling each role:
1. Economic Buyer — who controls the budget? What are their priorities (ROI, cost savings, strategic value)?
2. Champion — who inside wants this to succeed? What's their motivation?
3. User — who will actually use the product daily? What do they need vs what do they want?
4. Technical Evaluator — who assesses security, compliance, integration? What are their criteria?
5. Influencer — whose opinion carries weight but isn't a decision maker?
6. Blocker — who might resist this change? What's their concern?

For each stakeholder, capture: name/role, priorities, concerns, power level (low/medium/high), and engagement strategy. Summarise as a power-interest grid with recommended actions per quadrant.

items.title: B2B Product Requirements Document
items.summary: Structured PRD template tailored for B2B products with enterprise considerations
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Use this prompt to generate a structured PRD for a B2B feature or product, ensuring enterprise considerations like SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and SLA requirements are covered.

## Prompt

Act as a senior B2B product manager. Help me draft a Product Requirements Document by asking me questions one section at a time.

Section 1: Problem & Opportunity
- What business problem does this solve?
- How is it currently being solved (or not)?
- What's the market opportunity size?

Section 2: Target Persona & Segment
- Who is the primary buyer persona?
- Who are the end users?
- What company size/industry is this for?

Section 3: Requirements
- Functional requirements (list as user stories)
- Non-functional requirements: SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logging, data residency, SLA expectations, API rate limits
- Integration requirements: which third-party systems must integrate with?
- Security & compliance: SOC2, GDPR, HIPAA, ISO 27001?

Section 4: Success Metrics
- What leading indicators matter (adoption, activation)?
- What lagging indicators (retention, expansion revenue)?

Generate a clean PRD document from the answers.

items.title: B2B Competitive Intelligence Brief
items.summary: Systematic framework to research and document competitor positioning, strengths, and weaknesses in a B2B market
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Use this prompt when entering a new B2B market segment, facing a new competitor, or preparing for a product launch.

## Prompt

Act as a B2B competitive intelligence analyst. Guide me through building a competitive brief.

Step 1: Ask which market segment and which competitors to analyse (direct, indirect, emerging).

Step 2: For each competitor, gather:
- Company overview: funding, revenue range, headcount, founding year
- Product: core features, integrations, platform coverage
- Pricing:公开 tiers, enterprise pricing approach, contract terms
- Positioning: tagline, target customer, key differentiators claimed
- GTM: sales model (self-serve, inside sales, field sales), channel partners
- Strengths (from customer reviews and analyst reports)
- Weaknesses (from customer complaints, churn reasons)

Step 3: Build a competitive positioning matrix with axes (e.g. price vs features, ease of use vs power).

Step 4: Identify our strategic advantages and vulnerabilities.

Step 5: Recommend: what to emphasise in sales comparisons, what to build next to widen the gap, and what competitive risks to monitor.

items.title: B2B Onboarding Flow Designer
items.summary: Design an onboarding experience that gets B2B users to their first value moment quickly
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

B2B products often have complex setup requirements that delay time-to-value. Use this prompt to design or improve your onboarding flow.

## Prompt

Act as a B2B product growth specialist. Help me design an onboarding flow by asking questions.

Start by asking about the product and its core value proposition: what is the single most important action a new user must take to experience value?

Then ask about:
1. Setup complexity: does the product require SSO config, data import, team invitation, API keys?
2. User roles: who sets up vs who uses? Is there an admin who configures and end users who consume?
3. Current onboarding: what does the first session look like today? What's the drop-off rate?
4. Time-to-value: how long from signup to first meaningful action?

Then design:
- Day 0: welcome + guided setup (minimal required steps)
- Day 1: first value moment triggered
- Week 1: habit loop established
- Month 1: expansion triggers (invite team, upgrade)

For each phase, define: what the user does, what the product does, and what signals show success.

items.title: B2B User Persona Generator
items.summary: Generate detailed B2B buyer and user personas from market research data
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Generate detailed B2B personas for your target segments — both the economic buyer and the end user, who are often different people in B2B.

## Prompt

Act as a UX researcher specialised in B2B. Guide me through creating two distinct personas for my product.

First, the Economic Buyer persona:
- Job title and seniority level
- Department and reporting structure
- Goals: what business outcomes are they measured on?
- Pain points: what keeps them up at night?
- Decision criteria: what factors determine their vendor choice?
- Objections: what would make them say no?
- Information sources: where do they learn about solutions?

Second, the End User persona:
- Daily workflow related to the product
- Technical proficiency level
- Goals: what makes their job easier?
- Frustrations: what slows them down?
- Influence level on purchase decision
- Adoption barriers: what would prevent them from using the product?

Finally, create a comparison highlighting where the two personas' goals align and where they conflict, and recommend messaging for each.

items.title: B2B Churn Root Cause Analysis
items.summary: Systematic framework to investigate and diagnose why B2B customers churn
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Use when churn rates are increasing or a significant customer has churned. This prompt walks through data gathering, hypothesis generation, and root cause identification.

## Prompt

Act as a B2B customer success analyst. Help me investigate churn by asking questions.

Phase 1: Gather Data
- What is the overall churn rate and how has it trended?
- Which segments (by size, industry, plan) have highest churn?
- What is the average time-to-churn?
- What were the top 3 stated reasons in exit surveys?

Phase 2: Analyse Usage Patterns
- How did usage trend in the 90 days before churn?
- Which features did the churned cohort use vs retained?
- Was there a drop in login frequency, API calls, or team member activity?
- Did the customer have a dedicated CSM? How many touchpoints?

Phase 3: Interview Analysis
- What themes emerge from churn interviews?
- Are there common phrases like 'too expensive', 'not using it', 'switched to X'?

Phase 4: Root Cause Summary
Classify causes: Pricing, Product Gaps, Onboarding Failure, Support Quality, Competition, Internal Changes at Customer

Provide an action plan: quick wins (next 30 days), medium-term fixes (next quarter), strategic changes (next 6 months).

items.title: B2B API Product Specification
items.summary: Structured prompt to design an API product for B2B consumption, including endpoints, authentication, and developer experience
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Use when designing or scoping a public API for B2B customers, especially when the API is a product in its own right.

## Prompt

Act as an API product manager. Help me design a B2B API product.

Section 1: API Context
- What business capability does this API expose?
- Who are the primary developers consuming this API?
- Is this a public, partner-only, or internal API?

Section 2: Auth & Security
- Authentication method: API keys, OAuth 2.0, mutual TLS?
- Rate limiting: requests per minute/hour/day?
- Data privacy: what data can be returned? Any PII restrictions?

Section 3: Endpoints
- What are the core resources and their CRUD operations?
- What are the expected request/response shapes?
- Pagination, filtering, sorting approach?
- Webhook events for async workflows?

Section 4: Developer Experience
- SDKs needed for which languages?
- Documentation format: OpenAPI/Swagger?
- Sandbox environment? Rate limits for testing?
- SLAs: uptime guarantee, response time p99?
- Versioning strategy: URL path vs header versioning?

Section 5: Commercial Model
- Is the API free, usage-based, or tiered?
- How is usage metered and billed?
- What support SLAs come with each tier?

Provide a structured API product brief.

items.title: B2B Product Launch Checklist
items.summary: Comprehensive launch readiness checklist covering sales enablement, customer comms, support, and success metrics
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## When to use this

Use this structured prompt to build a complete B2B product launch plan covering all cross-functional dependencies.

## Prompt

Act as a B2B launch program manager. Guide me through building a launch checklist.

Start by asking: what are we launching (new product, feature, pricing change, or sunset)?

Then walk through each workstream:

Product Readiness
- Is the feature complete and tested?
- Are there known bugs with workarounds?
- Is documentation written?
- Is the API stable?

Sales Readiness
- Have sales been trained?
- Are battle cards updated?
- Is there a pricing sheet and contract addendum?
- Are demo environments ready?

Marketing Readiness
- Is there a landing page?
- Are case studies or testimonials ready?
- Is there an announcement blog post?
- Has the PR/comms plan been approved?

Customer Readiness
- Is there an in-app announcement?
- Is there an email sequence for existing customers?
- Are CSMs briefed on talking points?
- Is there a migration guide (if replacing existing functionality)?

Success Metrics
- What are the launch KPIs?
- What is the success criteria for week 1, month 1, quarter 1?
- What is the rollback plan if metrics aren't met?

Generate a timeline with owners and deadlines for each item.

items.title: B2B Value Proposition Design
items.summary: How to craft and test B2B value propositions that resonate with both economic buyers and end users
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

Crafting a B2B value proposition is different from B2C because you must appeal to at least two audiences: the economic buyer (ROI, efficiency, risk reduction) and the end user (usability, time saved, reduced frustration). A strong B2B value proposition bridges both.

## How to do it

**1. Map the value chain**
For each stakeholder in the buying decision, identify:
- What metric do they care about?
- How does your product improve it?
- How would they measure that improvement?

**2. Build a dual value proposition**
- Buyer message: "Reduce customer onboarding time by 40% with automated workflows"
- User message: "Set up custom onboarding sequences in minutes without engineering help"

**3. Quantify wherever possible**
- Instead of "improves efficiency", say "saves 12 hours per week per team member"
- Use customer case studies for proof points

**4. Test with the "So what?" drill**
For every claimed benefit, ask "So what?" three times until you reach a fundamental job-to-be-done.

**5. Create a value hypothesis and validate**
- Run customer interviews testing the message
- A/B test landing page copy
- Measure conversion from trial to paid

## When to use

- When launching a new product or feature
- When entering a new market segment
- When repositioning a mature product
- When sales teams report that prospects "don't get it"

items.title: B2B Customer Health Scoring
items.summary: Building and maintaining a customer health score system to predict churn and identify expansion opportunities
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

A customer health score is a composite metric that indicates the likelihood of retention, expansion, or churn for each B2B account. It combines product usage data, support interactions, and business signals into a single score.

## How to do it

**1. Define signal categories**

Product signals (40-50% weight):
- Login frequency trend (daily, weekly, monthly)
- Feature adoption breadth (number of features used / total available)
- Key action completion (did they reach the 'aha moment'?)
- API call volume trend

Support signals (20-30% weight):
- Ticket volume trend
- Severity distribution
- CSAT score from support interactions
- Time to resolution

Business signals (20-30% weight):
- Payment timeliness
- Contract length remaining
- Executive sponsor changes
- NPS score

**2. Set thresholds**
Green (80-100): healthy, likely to expand
Yellow (50-79): at risk, requires proactive outreach
Red (0-49): critical, intervention needed

**3. Automate and alert**
- Trigger alerts when a Green account drops to Yellow
- Flag accounts that have been Red for 30+ days
- Identify expansion candidates (high usage, approaching renewal)

**4. Review cadence**
- Automated daily scoring
- Weekly review of accounts that changed colour
- Monthly deep dive on Red accounts

## When to use

- When you have 50+ B2B accounts
- When churn is above 5% annually
- When CS team can't manually track every account

items.title: B2B Sales Enablement Asset Creation
items.summary: Creating effective sales enablement materials that help sales teams communicate product value
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

Sales enablement assets are materials that help your sales team effectively communicate your product's value, handle objections, and close deals. In B2B, this includes battle cards, pitch decks, comparison guides, and ROI calculators.

## How to do it

**1. Battle cards**
For each competitor, create a one-pager:
- Their positioning vs ours
- Key differentiation points (3-5)
- Common objections and rebuttals
- Where we lose (be honest) and how to handle it
- Ideal win scenarios: when we always beat them

**2. Pitch deck framework**
- Problem: the status quo gap (quantified)
- Solution: how we solve it (10 words or less)
- How it works: 3-step visual explanation
- Proof: customer logos, metrics, testimonials
- Business case: ROI summary, TCO comparison
- Next steps: trial, demo, POC offer

**3. ROI calculator**
- Build a simple spreadsheet model
- Inputs: number of users, current time spent, hourly cost
- Output: time saved, cost saved, productivity gain
- Make it interactive so reps can customise per prospect

**4. Competitive comparison guides**
- Feature comparison matrix
- Pricing comparison (apples-to-apples per seat/usage)
- Integration ecosystem comparison
- Security/compliance comparison (SOC2, GDPR, etc.)

## When to refresh

- After a product release
- When a competitor changes pricing or positioning
- Quarterly for active competitive landscapes

items.title: B2B Product Analytics & Metrics
items.summary: Choosing and tracking the right B2B product metrics across acquisition, activation, retention, and revenue
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

B2B product analytics focuses on account-level metrics rather than individual user metrics, since a single account often has multiple users. Key frameworks include the B2B version of AARRR (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Referral) with account-level aggregation.

## How to do it

**Account-level AARRR**

Acquisition:
- Number of new accounts by channel
- Cost per acquired account
- Time from lead to signup

Activation:
- Percentage of accounts that reach their first value moment
- Time to first value moment
- Accounts that invite team members in first week

Retention:
- Net revenue retention (NRR)
- Gross revenue retention (GRR)
- Account-level DAU/WAU/MAU
- Feature stickiness (% of accounts using feature weekly)

Revenue:
- ARR, ARPU, LTV
- Expansion revenue from upsells/cross-sells
- Logo churn rate
- Contraction rate (downgrades)

Referral:
- Net Promoter Score (account-level)
- Referral conversion rate

**Implementation tips**
- Instrument account_id on every event
- Use a warehouse-native analytics tool (dbt + Cube, or product analytics with account support)
- Build a weekly health dashboard for the product team
- Set explicit targets at the start of each quarter

## Common pitfalls

- Looking at user metrics alone (misleading when one account has 100 users)
- Not segmenting by account size (enterprise vs SMB behave differently)
- Vanity metrics (total logins) instead of actionable metrics (active accounts)

items.title: B2B Customer Advisory Board Management
items.summary: How to establish and run a Customer Advisory Board to get strategic input from key customers
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

A Customer Advisory Board (CAB) is a group of key customers who provide strategic input on product direction, market needs, and messaging. It's a B2B staple for building customer relationships and validating roadmap decisions.

## How to do it

**1. Recruitment**
- Invite 8-12 customers who represent your ideal customer profile
- Mix of champions and executive sponsors
- Ensure diversity of industry, company size, and use case
- Offer an incentive (annual meeting, executive access, early features)

**2. Structure**
- Term: 12-18 months with renewal option
- Meetings: 2x per year (in-person or virtual)
- Meeting format: strategy presentation, breakout discussion, product roadmap preview, feedback session
- Confidentiality: require NDA for early roadmap access

**3. Typical agenda**
- Market trends & industry insights from members
- Product roadmap preview and feedback
- Specific topic deep-dive (pricing, packaging, competitive positioning)
- Relationship building (dinner, networking)

**4. Managing output**
- Document every session with action items
- Close the feedback loop: tell CAB members what changed because of their input
- Track impact: count roadmap items influenced by CAB feedback

**5. Avoiding pitfalls**
- Don't let any single member dominate the agenda
- Don't share confidential information about other customers
- Don't treat it as a sales event — it's a strategy forum

## When to start

- When you have 20+ enterprise accounts
- When you need market validation for a major product bet
- When customer relationships need deepening beyond the quarterly business review

items.title: B2B Enterprise Sales Negotiation
items.summary: Key principles for product managers supporting enterprise sales negotiations including proof of concepts, security reviews, and contracting
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

B2B product managers often get pulled into enterprise sales cycles to support POCs, security reviews, and custom contracting. Understanding this process helps you accelerate deals and avoid over-committing the engineering team.

## How to do it

**1. Proof of Concept (POC) management**
- Define success criteria before starting: what must be true for the POC to pass?
- Set a fixed timeline (typically 2-6 weeks)
- Assign a technical point of contact from the prospect's team
- Weekly check-ins to track progress and address blockers
- Document results with a POC report: what worked, what didn't, next steps

**2. Security review support**
- Prepare a security packet upfront: SOC2 report, penetration test results, data processing agreement, subprocessor list
- Common B2B questions: encryption at rest and in transit, data residency, backup frequency, access controls
- Create a self-service security questionnaire to reduce back-and-forth

**3. Contract negotiation**
- Know your deal desk: what discounts can you approve without escalation?
- Understand contracting models: annual prepay vs monthly, committed vs consumption
- Common B2B terms: uptime SLA (99.9%), support response times, data retention after cancellation, mutual indemnification
- Work with legal to create standard contract templates with acceptable ranges

**4. Avoiding scope creep**
- Use a structured change order process for any custom work
- Distinguish between 'configuration' (partners, no code) and 'customisation' (engineering work, fee)
- Be present in late-stage meetings to catch last-minute feature requests masquerading as 'just a small thing'

## When to get involved

- When the deal is above a revenue threshold
- When the prospect is a strategic account
- When there are technical requirements that need product expertise
- When sales is asking for custom features

items.title: B2B Pricing & Packaging Strategy
items.summary: Frameworks for designing B2B pricing models and packaging features across tiers
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

B2B pricing is rarely a single number. It's a system of tiers, usage limits, and add-ons designed to capture value from different customer segments while leaving room for growth.

## How to do it

**1. Choose a pricing model**

Per-seat pricing: simplest, most common. Works well when value scales linearly with users.
- Example: $50/user/month, 5-user minimum

Usage-based pricing: customer pays for what they consume.
- Example: $0.10 per API call, $2 per processed document
- Pros: aligns cost with value, low barrier to entry
- Cons: revenue predictability is harder

Tiered + usage: base tier includes allocation, overage charged separately.
- Example: $500/month for 10,000 API calls, $0.05 per additional call

Value-based: priced on outcome delivered.
- Example: percentage of identified savings, flat fee per workflow automated

**2. Design your tiers**
- Tier 1 (Starter): low price, essential features, self-serve
- Tier 2 (Growth): moderate price, most features, some support
- Tier 3 (Business): higher price, all features, dedicated support
- Enterprise: custom pricing, SSO, audit logs, SLA, custom contract

**3. Good-better-best pricing psychology**
- The middle tier should be your best value — this is what most customers buy
- The top tier makes the middle look reasonable
- Feature gate strategically: must-have features in all tiers, nice-to-haves gated up

**4. Pricing review cadence**
- Quarterly: check competitors and market shifts
- Annually: review pricing strategy and potentially raise prices for existing customers (with grandfathering option)

items.title: B2B Go-to-Market Planning
items.summary: Building a B2B go-to-market plan including channel strategy, sales model, and launch sequencing
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

A B2B go-to-market (GTM) plan defines how you'll reach, acquire, and retain customers. It covers target segments, channel strategy, sales model, pricing, launch timeline, and success metrics.

## How to do it

**1. Define target segments**
- Ideal Customer Profile (ICP): industry, company size, maturity, tech stack
- Personas: buyer vs user, their priorities, where they spend time
- Total Addressable Market (TAM): number of accounts × average contract value

**2. Choose sales model**
- Self-serve: signup, trial, credit card — works for SMB, low ACV (<$5K)
- Inside sales: inbound leads + outbound calls — works for mid-market ($5K-$50K)
- Field sales: enterprise reps, relationship-driven — works for enterprise ($50K+)
- Channel/partners: resellers, MSPs, integrations — extends reach

**3. Channel strategy**
- Direct: website, content marketing, paid ads, sales team
- Indirect: partners, agencies, marketplaces, referrals
- Pick primary and secondary channels based on cost per acquired account

**4. Launch phases**
- Beta: 5-10 design partners, high-touch, focused on product feedback
- Early access: 50-100 accounts, monitored onboarding, case studies created
- General availability: full marketing push, sales team trained, self-serve enabled
- Scale: channel expansion, international, enterprise sales motion

**5. Metrics to track**
- CAC (customer acquisition cost) by channel
- LTV/CAC ratio (target: 3x+)
- Time to close by segment
- Pipeline velocity
- Win rate by source

items.title: B2B Compliance & Security Readiness
items.summary: Understanding and preparing for B2B compliance requirements including SOC 2, GDPR, and enterprise security reviews
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

Enterprise B2B buyers require proof of security and compliance before purchasing. SOC 2 Type II is the baseline, with HIPAA, ISO 27001, and GDPR being common asks depending on your market.

## How to do it

**1. SOC 2 readiness**
- SOC 2 Type I: point-in-time audit (3-6 months prep)
- SOC 2 Type II: controls operated over 6-12 months
- Common trust principles: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy
- Most B2B SaaS starts with Security + Confidentiality
- Tools: Vanta, Drata, Secureframe automate evidence collection

**2. GDPR compliance**
- Data Processing Agreement (DPA) for EU customers
- Data residency options (US, EU)
- Data deletion and export API
- Cookie consent and privacy policy
- Data Protection Officer contact

**3. Security review packet**
Create a reusable packet with:
- SOC 2 report (latest)
- Penetration test results (annual)
- Vulnerability management policy
- Incident response plan
- Subprocessor list and DPA
- Encryption: TLS 1.2+ in transit, AES-256 at rest
- Access control: SSO/SAML, RBAC, MFA, session management
- Backup frequency and disaster recovery plan

**4. Building security into product**
- Authentication: SSO/SAML is a table-stakes requirement for enterprise
- Authorization: RBAC with ability to create custom roles
- Audit logging: who did what, when, from where — retained minimum 90 days
- Data retention: configurable retention period, bulk deletion API
- API security: rate limiting, IP whitelisting, API key rotation

## When to invest

- SOC 2: when first enterprise customer asks for it (usually between 5-20 employees)
- GDPR: when you have EU customers (or plan to)
- HIPAA: only if selling to healthcare

items.title: B2B Product-Led Growth Foundations
items.summary: Applying product-led growth principles in a B2B context with a free trial, self-serve onboarding, and virality
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

Product-led growth (PLG) means the product itself drives acquisition, retention, and expansion — rather than a sales team. In B2B, PLG works best for products with low switching costs, clear individual value, and collaborative team features.

## How to do it

**1. Self-serve signup flow**
- No sales call required to start using the product
- Email or SSO signup, automatic workspace creation
- Immediate access to core features (not a gated demo)
- Time-to-value: under 5 minutes from signup to first success

**2. Free tier or trial design**
- Free tier: limited features or usage, no time limit
- Time-limited trial: full features for 14-30 days
- Usage-limited trial: free up to an action count, then upgrade
- Best approach: free tier with generous limits, then paid beyond

**3. Team virality**
- Build collaboration into the core experience
- Make it easy to invite teammates (and show value of having them)
- Shared workspaces, collaborative documents, team dashboards
- When teammates join, the original user's stickiness increases

**4. Expansion triggers**
- Usage approaching plan limits
- Number of team members approaching plan cap
- Feature discovery prompts: 'Want advanced analytics? Upgrade to Growth plan'
- Time-based: send upgrade prompts after N days of active use

**5. B2B PLG + sales hybrid**
- PLG handles SMB and self-serve motion
- Sales handles enterprise leads (triggered by domain-based routing or usage thresholds)
- PQL (product-qualified lead): account hits activation milestone → sales outreach

## Common mistakes

- Making signup too complex (enterprise features up front)
- Not having a clear 'aha moment' defined
- Trying PLG with a product that requires heavy configuration or training
- Ignoring account-level analytics (treating each user independently)

items.title: B2B Requirements Prioritisation
items.summary: Frameworks for prioritising B2B feature requests across many stakeholders with conflicting needs
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it is

In B2B, you'll receive conflicting feature requests from sales (closing deals), support (retention), executives (strategy), and customers (their specific needs). A structured prioritisation framework helps you make defensible decisions.

## How to do it

**1. Opportunity scoring**
For each request, score 1-5 on:
- Revenue impact: how much ACV or pipeline does this unlock?
- Customer count: how many accounts need this?
- Strategic alignment: does it support our product vision?
- Engineering effort: how complex is it to build? (inverse score)
- Risk: does not doing this cause churn?

**2. RICE framework (B2B adapted)**
- Reach: how many accounts per quarter?
- Impact: revenue per account (low/medium/high with numeric multiplier)
- Confidence: how sure are we of the estimates?
- Effort: engineering person-weeks

**3. ICE framework (for growth experiments)**
- Impact on metric
- Confidence it will work
- Ease of implementation

**4. Outcome-driven roadmap**
Instead of feature backlog, define desired outcomes:
- 'Increase 30-day activation rate from 40% to 60%'
- 'Reduce time-to-first-value from 14 days to 3 days'
- 'Improve NRR from 95% to 110%'

**5. Saying no gracefully**
- Explain the trade-off: 'We chose X over Y because it serves 3x more customers'
- Use the roadmap as your 'no' document — if it's not on the roadmap, the answer is 'not now'
- Offer alternatives: workaround, integration, partner solution
- Keep a 'backlog' but be transparent that it's an ideas list, not a commitment

items.title: Gong Revenue Intelligence
items.summary: AI-powered platform that captures and analyses customer calls to uncover buying signals, objections, and competitive intelligence
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Gong records, transcribes, and analyses sales calls, product demos, and customer meetings. For B2B product managers, it's a goldmine of unfiltered customer feedback — real objections, feature requests in context, competitive mentions, and how customers actually talk about your product.

## Suggested workflow

1. Ask sales to share access or set up automated deal-level sharing
2. Search for key terms: your product name, competitor names, specific feature requests
3. Filter by deal stage to understand how conversations change through the buying process
4. Listen to calls where deals were lost to understand competitive positioning gaps
5. Extract themes quarterly and feed into your product roadmap prioritisation

items.title: Amplitude for B2B Product Analytics
items.summary: Product analytics platform with account-level analysis, behavioural cohorts, and experimentation for B2B products
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Amplitude helps B2B product teams understand how entire accounts (not just individual users) engage with their product. Key features: account-level charts, behavioural cohorts, funnel analysis, retention analysis, and A/B testing.

## Suggested workflow

1. Instrument account_id on every event from day one
2. Define account-level 'active' status (e.g. 5+ users active in a week)
3. Build activation funnels at account level: signup → setup → invite team → first value
4. Create behavioural cohorts: accounts that use Feature A → do they retain better?
5. Set up account health scoring using Amplitude's predictive features
6. Run experiments on onboarding flow, pricing page, or feature discovery

items.title: Intercom for B2B Customer Communication
items.summary: Customer communication platform with in-app messaging, chatbots, product tours, and help centre for B2B SaaS
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Intercom enables B2B product teams to communicate with customers inside the product through messages, product tours, and a help centre. Product managers use it to: onboard new accounts with guided tours, collect in-product feedback, send targeted announcements about new features, and identify accounts needing attention based on behaviour.

## Suggested workflow

1. Set up a welcome series for new accounts with a 3-step product tour
2. Create targeted messages based on account plan type and usage behaviour
3. Build a help centre with searchable documentation tied to product context
4. Use in-app surveys for feature feedback and NPS
5. Set up alerts for accounts showing signs of churn (no logins in 14 days)
6. Analyse support ticket topics quarterly to identify product improvement opportunities

items.title: Mixpanel for Product Analytics
items.summary: Product analytics with account-level insights, session replay, and feature adoption tracking for B2B products
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Mixpanel tracks user and account behaviour across your product. For B2B PMs, its account-level reporting and session replay features help understand how teams adopt your product. Key strengths: flexible event tracking, powerful segmentation, data visualisation, and mobile SDK support.

## Suggested workflow

1. Instrument your product with Mixpanel SDK, tagging all key actions
2. Define account-level metrics: accounts active, feature adoption per account, account retention
3. Build funnels for critical flows: invite flow, setup wizard, first API call
4. Use session replay to watch how real users (anonymised) navigate your product
5. Create cohorts to compare behaviour of retained vs churned accounts
6. Set up dashboards for weekly product health review

items.title: Salesforce for B2B CRM and Pipeline
items.summary: Enterprise CRM for tracking B2B sales pipeline, account management, and product-influenced deal insights
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Salesforce is the ubiquitous B2B CRM. For product managers, it helps connect product decisions to revenue outcomes: which deals are being influenced by which features, what objections are closing or losing deals, and how product changes affect pipeline velocity.

## Suggested workflow

1. Ensure product feedback fields are added to Opportunity objects (feature interest, competitor mentioned, primary objection)
2. Build a dashboard showing: deals won/lost by feature request, competitive win/loss rates, and average deal size by product area
3. Integrate with product analytics (Amplitude/Mixpanel) to correlate product engagement with deal stage
4. Work with sales ops to create automated alerts when a strategic deal hits an objection your product can address
5. Quarterly: review lost deal reasons and feed into product roadmap 
6. Use Einstein Analytics for predictive insights on which accounts are likely to expand or churn based on product usage

items.title: FigJam for B2B Product Workshops
items.summary: Collaborative whiteboarding tool for remote B2B product workshops including stakeholder mapping, opportunity sizing, and roadmap planning
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

FigJam (by Figma) is an online whiteboard tool perfect for B2B product management workshops: persona mapping sessions, opportunity solution trees, stakeholder influence mapping, and roadmap visualisation. Its template library includes many product management frameworks.

## Suggested workflow

1. Use the Personas template to build B2B buyer and user personas collaboratively
2. Run opportunity solution tree workshops: start with desired outcome → explore opportunities → propose solutions → test assumptions
3. Facilitate stakeholder mapping sessions with Sales, CS, and Support teams
4. Visualise the buying journey: from awareness to signed contract to onboarded account
5. Export workshop outcomes to product documentation or directly to your Linear/Notion backlog
6. Share with remote teams asynchronously using timestamped comments

items.title: Pendo for In-App Guidance and Analytics
items.summary: Product experience platform with in-app guides, feature adoption analytics, and feedback collection for B2B SaaS
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Pendo helps B2B product teams understand feature adoption at account level and drive user behaviour through in-app guides, tooltips, and walkthroughs. For B2B PMs, its account-level analytics tie product usage directly to account health.

## Suggested workflow

1. Tag your UI elements to track feature usage per account
2. Create a product adoption dashboard: feature usage trends, stickiness ratios, top accounts by engagement
3. Build in-app guides for new feature launches: targeted tooltips that only appear for relevant accounts
4. Use polls and NPS surveys to collect feedback inside the product
5. Set up 'paths' analysis to see how accounts navigate onboarding vs power users
6. Identify feature drop-off and create re-engagement campaigns

items.title: Canny for B2B Feature Requests
items.summary: Dedicated customer feedback board for collecting, prioritising, and communicating about B2B feature requests
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Canny provides a public or private feedback board where B2B customers can submit and vote on feature requests. It replaces the inbox flood of 'can you add X?' with a structured, transparent system that helps prioritisation.

## Suggested workflow

1. Set up a public portal (or private per-account boards for enterprise)
2. Let customers submit ideas with categories and tags
3. Enable voting (upvote, not a score — one vote per account to avoid gaming)
4. Link each request to a Linear issue for traceability
5. Use status labels: Under Review, Planned, In Progress, Shipped, Declined
6. Close the loop: comment on every request explaining the decision rationale
7. Review quarterly: top-voted requests become input for roadmap planning
8. Integrate with Slack for internal notifications on high-impact requests

items.title: Hotjar for B2B UX Research
items.summary: Behaviour analytics platform with session recordings, heatmaps, and in-product surveys for B2B UX improvements
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

Hotjar provides session recordings, heatmaps, and in-product surveys that help B2B product managers understand how users navigate complex enterprise workflows. It reveals where users get stuck, which UI elements get ignored, and what confuses new users during onboarding.

## Suggested workflow

1. Install the tracking snippet across your product
2. Set up funnels to identify where users drop off in key B2B flows (e.g., integration setup, team invitation, billing configuration)
3. Watch session recordings of: first-time users, users who triggered errors, and power users exploring advanced features
4. Deploy exit-intent surveys to understand why visitors didn't convert
5. Use heatmaps on pricing and documentation pages to see what questions users have
6. Create feedback widgets on specific pages for contextual input
7. Compile quarterly UX audit based on recording patterns and survey responses

items.title: User Interviews for B2B Research
items.summary: Platform for recruiting, scheduling, and managing B2B user research participants
items.author: MILO Team
items.body:
## What it helps with

User Interviews is a platform for recruiting research participants. For B2B product managers, it solves the hardest part of user research: finding qualified participants from your target market (by title, industry, company size, tech stack) and scheduling interviews without the back-and-forth.

## Suggested workflow

1. Define your screener criteria: job title, seniority, industry, company size, current tools used
2. Create a research project with your target participant count and incentives
3. Use the platform's panel or your own customer list to recruit
4. Automate scheduling with calendar sync and reminders
5. Conduct interviews (record via Zoom/Meet built-in)
6. Use the tool's tagging and note features to capture key findings
7. Export insights to your research repository (Dovetail, Condens, or Notion)

items.title: Escaping the Build Trap
items.summary: How effective product management creates organisations that ship the right things, with strong B2B product organisation examples
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Melissa Perri
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Melissa Perri provides a comprehensive framework for building product-led organisations. For B2B PMs, the chapters on outcome vs output, product strategy, and structuring product teams are directly applicable. The case studies feature B2B companies navigating the transition from project-based to product-based thinking.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers at any level, especially those in organisations transitioning to product-led

## Key takeaway

Stop measuring success by shipping features. Define business outcomes, build a product strategy that connects those outcomes to customer needs, and structure your teams to deliver value continuously.

items.title: Inspired: How to Create Products Customers Love
items.summary: The definitive guide to product management with dedicated sections on B2B enterprise product discovery and delivery
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Marty Cagan
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Marty Cagan's book is widely considered the product management bible. The second half of the book specifically addresses B2B and enterprise product management, including chapters on sales-driven vs product-driven companies, managing stakeholders, and running product discovery with enterprise customers.

## Best for

All product managers; essential reading for anyone working on B2B products

## Key takeaway

Great products come from empowered product teams that combine deep customer empathy with business understanding and technology. Discovery (prototyping and testing) is just as important as delivery.

items.title: Crossing the Chasm
items.summary: Classic framework for taking B2B technology products from early adopters to mainstream market
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Geoffrey A. Moore
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Crossing the Chasm remains the definitive playbook for B2B technology adoption. Moore's model of the technology adoption lifecycle — innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, laggards — and the 'chasm' between early adopters and early majority is essential reading for any B2B product manager launching a new product or entering a new market.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers launching new products or entering new segments

## Key takeaway

Focus on a single beachhead segment and build a 'whole product' solution before expanding. Don't try to serve everyone at once — you'll serve no one well.

items.title: The Mom Test
items.summary: Practical guide to conducting honest customer conversations that reveal real needs, especially relevant for B2B discovery
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Rob Fitzpatrick
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

The Mom Test is a short, practical book about how to avoid false positives in customer conversations. For B2B PMs, its lessons on asking about specific past behaviour (not hypothetical future intent), talking about money early, and avoiding 'compliments' that waste your time are invaluable when doing discovery with busy enterprise customers.

## Best for

Product Managers, founders, and anyone conducting customer interviews

## Key takeaway

Don't ask if they'd buy your idea. Ask about their current workflow, what they've tried before, and whether they've spent money solving this problem. Real commitments (time, money, reputation) are the only signals that matter.

items.title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy
items.summary: Framework for developing coherent strategy with focus on diagnosing challenges and creating coordinated action
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Richard Rumelt
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Rumelt provides a clear, actionable definition of what strategy actually is: a diagnosis of the challenge, a guiding policy, and coherent actions. For B2B PMs, this framework helps differentiate between genuine product strategy and vague aspirations like 'grow market share'.

## Best for

Senior Product Managers, Product Directors, and anyone responsible for product strategy

## Key takeaway

Strategy identifies the key challenge, sets a clear direction, and coordinates actions to overcome that challenge. Bad strategy is fluff: it fails to define the problem and confuses goals with strategy.

items.title: The Lean Startup
items.summary: Build-measure-learn methodology adapted for B2B with enterprise validation, pivots, and innovation accounting
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Eric Ries
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

While examples skew B2C, the core concepts — build-measure-learn, minimum viable product, innovation accounting, and pivot-or-persevere — are directly applicable to B2B. The key adaptation is that your MVP with enterprise customers might be a concierge service or a manual process that delivers value while you learn.

## Best for

Product Managers working on new products, features, or entering new markets

## Key takeaway

Validate your riskiest assumptions first. Ship a minimal version that tests your hypothesis, measure customer behaviour, learn whether to pivot or persevere. Speed of learning is the competitive advantage.

items.title: Hacking Growth
items.summary: Growth hacking frameworks applied to B2B with account-level acquisition, activation, and expansion tactics
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Sean Ellis & Morgan Brown
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

The book provides a structured approach to growth: building a growth team, identifying growth levers, running experiments, and scaling what works. For B2B PMs, the chapters on activation loops and retention engines (rather than just acquisition) are particularly useful.

## Best for

Product Managers working on growth, activation, or retention

## Key takeaway

Growth is not a one-time campaign — it's a continuous process of experimentation built into how your team operates. Focus on the 'aha moment' that makes customers stick and build retention loops before scaling acquisition.

items.title: Competing Against Luck
items.summary: Jobs-to-be-done framework for understanding why customers hire and fire products, with B2B examples
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Clayton Christensen
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Christensen's Jobs-to-be-Done theory is a powerful lens for B2B product management. Instead of focusing on demographics or features, ask: what 'job' does the customer hire your product to do? The B2B examples show how understanding the progress a customer wants to make (not just their functional need) leads to breakthrough products.

## Best for

Product Managers looking for a customer-needs-first framework

## Key takeaway

Customers don't buy products; they 'hire' them to make progress in a specific circumstance. Understanding the functional, emotional, and social dimensions of that job reveals opportunities competitors miss.

items.title: The Challenger Sale
items.summary: Research-backed sales methodology for complex B2B deals that product managers should understand to align product and sales
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Matthew Dixon & Brent Adamson
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

CEB research found that the most effective B2B sales reps don't build relationships — they challenge the customer's thinking. For B2B PMs, understanding this helps you create sales enablement materials that teach, tailor, and take control of the conversation, rather than just listing features.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers working closely with sales teams

## Key takeaway

The most effective B2B sales approach is to teach prospects something new about their business, tailor the message to their specific context, and take control of the sales conversation with commercial teaching.

items.title: Continuous Discovery Habits
items.summary: Practical habits for running ongoing product discovery with B2B customers including opportunity trees and structured interviews
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Teresa Torres
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Teresa Torres provides a structured, weekly cadence for product discovery that works for B2B teams. The book covers opportunity solution trees, structured customer interviews, and how to integrate discovery with delivery. For B2B PMs with limited access to customers, the interviewing and synthesising methods are especially practical.

## Best for

Product Managers who want a systematic approach to discovery

## Key takeaway

Discovery is not a phase — it's a continuous habit. Map desired outcomes to opportunities to solutions, interview customers weekly (even 15-minute calls), and visualise your thinking with opportunity solution trees.

items.title: B2B Product Discovery with Enterprise Customers
items.summary: How Teresa Torres adapts continuous discovery practices for long-cycle enterprise B2B sales environments
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Teresa Torres / Product Talk
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Teresa Torres, author of Continuous Discovery Habits, addresses the specific challenge of doing discovery in B2B contexts where you have limited access to customers, long sales cycles, and multiple stakeholders per account.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers struggling to get regular customer access

## Key takeaway

You don't need massive sample sizes — 4-6 well-structured interviews per quarter with the right stakeholders can surface 90%+ of the critical insights. Focus on recent, specific behaviour, not opinions.

items.title: Why B2B Products Die: The Feature Fallacy
items.summary: Why adding more features hurts B2B products and what to do instead
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Marty Cagan / SVPG
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Marty Cagan explains why the 'feature team' model — where product managers just take orders from sales and stakeholders — leads to bloated, unloved B2B products. He makes the case for empowered product teams focused on outcomes.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers in sales-driven organisations

## Key takeaway

Stop measuring your team by how many features they ship. Measure by business outcomes achieved. Empower your team to solve problems, not just implement stakeholder requests.

items.title: Shape Up: Building B2B Products in Six-Week Cycles
items.summary: Ryan Singer explains how Basecamp's Shape Up methodology applies to B2B product development
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Ryan Singer / 37signals
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Ryan Singer walks through how Shape Up — a product development methodology from Basecamp — works for B2B products. He covers shaping, betting, and building in six-week cycles with a cool-down period.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers looking for an alternative to Scrum/Kanban

## Key takeaway

Fixed time, variable scope. Define the 'appetite' (how much time to spend) and shape the problem to fit within it. If it won't fit, don't start — wait until a smaller version emerges.

items.title: B2B Product-Led Growth vs Sales-Led: When and How
items.summary: OpenView Partners' analysis of when to choose product-led growth vs sales-led for B2B products
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Kyle Poyar / OpenView
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Kyle Poyar (formerly OpenView) breaks down the key differences between product-led and sales-led GTM motions, and importantly, how to combine them. He uses examples from Calendly, Canva, and Expensify to show how PLG works in practice.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers evaluating GTM strategy for their product

## Key takeaway

Product-led and sales-led are not mutually exclusive. Many successful B2B companies start product-led for land and add sales-led for expand. Let the product qualify leads, then bring in sales for high-value deals.

items.title: From Zero to Enterprise: B2B SaaS Product Journey
items.summary: How to evolve your B2B product from SMB self-serve to enterprise-grade with SSO, RBAC, and compliance
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Elena Verna / Amplitude
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Elena Verna (former SVP Growth at Amplitude, now at Dropbox) shares her framework for taking a B2B product upmarket. She covers when to add enterprise features, how to balance product-led with sales-led, and the metrics that matter at each stage.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers planning an upmarket move

## Key takeaway

Don't build enterprise features before you have enterprise demand. Let customers pay for what they need: start with self-serve, add a growth tier with premium features, then negotiate enterprise contracts with custom requirements.

items.title: B2B SaaS Metrics that Matter
items.summary: David Skok's classic presentation on SaaS metrics with emphasis on B2B unit economics
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: David Skok / Matrix Partners
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

David Skok's 'SaaS Metrics 2.0' presentation is a masterclass in B2B SaaS unit economics. He explains CAC, LTV, churn, and payback period with clear examples and shows how these metrics interact to determine whether a business is healthy or dying.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers who want to understand the business side of product decisions

## Key takeaway

The three levers of B2B SaaS success: reduce churn, increase customer acquisition, and improve unit economics. All product decisions should ultimately improve at least one of these.

items.title: How to Build an Enterprise B2B Product Team
items.summary: Insights on structuring product teams for enterprise B2B including managing stakeholders and sales relationships
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Leah Tharin / Product Coalition
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Leah Tharin, an experienced B2B product leader, discusses the unique challenges of building and running product teams in enterprise B2B environments. She covers stakeholder management, balancing customer requests with strategy, and hiring for B2B PM roles.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers aspiring to leadership roles or building product organisations

## Key takeaway

In B2B, the product team must deeply understand the sales motion, the implementation process, and the customer success lifecycle — because the product experience spans the entire customer journey, not just the UI.

items.title: The Art of the B2B Product Roadmap
items.summary: How to create and communicate product roadmaps in B2B environments with multiple stakeholders
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Janna Bastow / ProdPad
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Janna Bastow (co-founder of ProdPad and Mind the Product) explains how to build B2B product roadmaps that balance transparency with strategic flexibility. She covers the now-next-later framework and how to handle the 'where is my feature?' question from enterprise customers.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers who struggle with roadmap communication

## Key takeaway

A roadmap is a strategic communication tool, not a delivery schedule. Use outcome-based themes (not feature lists) and the now-next-later framework to show direction without over-committing.

items.title: Pricing B2B SaaS: Psychology and Strategy
items.summary: Deep dive on B2B SaaS pricing psychology, tier design, and packaging strategy
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Patrick Campbell / ProfitWell (now Paddle)
items.body:
## Why it is worth watching

Patrick Campbell, founder of ProfitWell (now Paddle), presents a data-driven approach to B2B pricing based on thousands of SaaS pricing analyses. He covers value metrics, tier structure, anchoring, decoy effects, and how to raise prices without losing customers.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers who influence pricing decisions

## Key takeaway

Your pricing model is a product decision. The right value metric aligns what customers pay with the value they receive. Test pricing changes with statistical rigour — your intuition about price elasticity is almost certainly wrong.

items.title: SaaStr Annual
items.summary: The largest conference for B2B SaaS founders, executives, and product leaders covering growth, fundraising, and operations
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: SaaStr / Jason Lemkin
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

SaaStr Annual is a massive B2B SaaS conference with 10,000+ attendees. It covers the full stack: product, sales, marketing, fundraising, and customer success. For B2B product managers, the product-specific tracks and peer networking are invaluable.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers looking to network, learn from peers, and stay current on SaaS best practices

## What to expect

Expect hundreds of sessions across multiple tracks, keynote talks from top B2B SaaS leaders (CEO roundtables), product management focused workshops, and extensive networking opportunities.

items.title: Mind the Product
items.summary: Leading product management conference with strong B2B content including enterprise product discovery and strategy tracks
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Mind the Product / Pendo
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

Mind the Product is one of the premier product management conferences globally. Their programming usually includes strong B2B-specific talks covering product discovery in enterprise contexts, outcome-driven roadmaps, and scaling product organisations.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers at all levels who want to invest in their craft

## What to expect

A mix of keynote talks, breakout sessions, and workshops. Topics range from tactical (writing good user stories for B2B) to strategic (building product orgs). Excellent networking with 1500+ product professionals.

items.title: ProductWorld
items.summary: Product management conference with dedicated enterprise/B2B track focusing on strategy, AI in product, and leadership
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Product World / Product School
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

ProductWorld brings together product leaders from major B2B companies. The enterprise track covers B2B-specific topics: product-led sales, enterprise stakeholder management, and navigating complex buyer journeys.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers interested in product strategy, AI-powered products, and leadership

## What to expect

Keynotes from CPOs at major B2B companies, hands-on workshops on product strategy and AI integration, enterprise track with dedicated B2B content, and certification credit for Product School alumni.

items.title: Pulse (by Gainsight)
items.summary: Customer success and product-led growth conference essential for B2B product managers focused on retention and expansion
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Gainsight
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

Pulse is Gainsight's customer success conference but has become increasingly product-focused as the lines between product and CS blur in B2B. Sessions cover: product-led growth strategies, customer health scoring, NRR expansion tactics, and the product-CS feedback loop.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers working on retention, growth, and customer success alignment


## What to expect

Case studies from companies like Zoom, Box, and Salesforce on how they drive growth through customer success, product-CS alignment workshops, and networking with customer success leaders.

items.title: Config (by Figma)
items.summary: Figma's annual design conference with strong product management content including design systems and collaboration tools for B2B
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Figma
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

While Config is Figma's design conference, it has become increasingly relevant for B2B product managers. Topics include: design systems at scale (especially relevant for B2B products with complex UIs), collaborative product development, and AI in product design.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers working closely with design teams or on design-rich products

## What to expect

Product design showcases from major B2B companies, workshops on design systems and prototyping, sessions on how AI is changing product design workflows, and access to Figma's product team for roadmap discussions.

items.title: ProductCon
items.summary: Multi-city product management conference with workshops on B2B strategy, discovery, and execution
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Product School
items.location: San Francisco, CA, USA (also NYC, London, virtual)
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

ProductCon is a day-long product management conference held in multiple cities worldwide. It features hands-on workshops and talks from product leaders at companies like Google, Meta, Airbnb, and Stripe — many with B2B-specific case studies.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers looking for practical, actionable takeaways

## What to expect

Full-day conference with keynotes, breakout sessions, and workshops. Topics vary by location but typically include: product strategy, discovery techniques, stakeholder management, and career growth for PMs.

items.title: Enterprise Sales & B2B Product Summit
items.summary: Focused event bridging B2B product management and enterprise sales for product-led growth
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Product-Led Alliance
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

The Product-Led Summit by ProductLed focuses specifically on combining product-led growth with enterprise sales motions. Sessions cover: hybrid go-to-market strategies, pricing for PLG + enterprise, and product-qualified lead (PQL) frameworks.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers building or transitioning to a product-led GTM model

## What to expect

Case studies from PLG-first B2B companies (Calendly, Webflow, Notion), practical workshops on PLG implementation, and deep dives into how to layer enterprise sales on top of self-serve.

items.title: Rise of the Product-Led Enterprise
items.summary: Conference dedicated to B2B enterprise product-led growth with sessions on pricing, onboarding, and team structures
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: OpenView Partners
items.body:
## Why it is worth attending

OpenView's annual product-led growth event brings together B2B founders, product leaders, and investors. The content is heavily focused on product-led growth in enterprise contexts: how to land with self-serve and expand with sales.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers and leaders at growth-stage companies

## What to expect

Data-driven keynotes on PLG benchmarks (from OpenView's extensive research), breakout sessions on pricing, product analytics, and growth experiments, and networking with 300+ product leaders.

items.title: B2B Product-Led Certification (ProductLed)
items.summary: Comprehensive certification course on applying product-led growth principles in B2B SaaS companies
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: ProductLed / Wes Bush
items.body:
## Why it is worth taking

This certification course by Wes Bush (author of Product-Led Growth) provides a structured, step-by-step framework for implementing PLG in B2B SaaS. It covers: identifying your 'aha moment', building a self-serve funnel, and creating expansion loops.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers new to PLG or building a PLG motion from scratch

## Key takeaway

A structured, module-based course with templates, worksheets, and real-world examples. The certification demonstrates you can apply PLG frameworks to a live product.

items.title: Enterprise Design Thinking Practitioner (IBM)
items.summary: IBM's enterprise-focused design thinking certification adapted for complex B2B product development
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: IBM
items.body:
## Why it is worth taking

Unlike generic design thinking, IBM's version is built specifically for enterprise contexts. It addresses the complexity of B2B: multiple stakeholders per project, long feedback cycles, and the need to align with broader business strategy.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers working on complex products with multiple stakeholder groups

## Key takeaway

The course teaches a 'loop' model (Observe-Reflect-Make) rather than a linear process, and introduces 'sponsor users' — a concept for getting direct access to real customers inside enterprise organisations.

items.title: Product-Led Growth Certificate (Product School)
items.summary: Product School's certification covering PLG strategies specifically for B2B SaaS products
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Product School
items.body:
## Why it is worth taking

Product School is one of the leading product management education providers. Their PLG certification covers how to apply product-led growth strategies to B2B products, including: building a viral loop, monetising free users, and creating a growth team.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers looking to add a recognised certification and learn a structured PLG framework

## Key takeaway

A practical, hands-on course taught by experienced product leaders with real B2B case studies. You'll build an actual PLG strategy for a product during the course.

items.title: Reforge: Product Strategy for B2B
items.summary: Reforge's advanced program on B2B product strategy including tiered pricing, enterprise feature prioritisation, and PLG motion design
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Reforge
items.body:
## Why it is worth taking

Reforge's programs are advanced, cohort-based, and taught by experienced product leaders. The product strategy program covers B2B-specific topics: how to choose your target segment, build a tiered pricing model, manage enterprise stakeholder relationships, and evolve your product from SMB to enterprise.

## Best for

Senior B2B Product Managers, Heads of Product, and CPOs

## Key takeaway

Reforge programs are not for beginners. They assume you have 5+ years of experience and focus on frameworks you can apply immediately. The peer cohort is as valuable as the content itself.

items.title: How to Sell Enterprise B2B SaaS (SaaStr Course)
items.summary: SaaStr's practical course on enterprise sales fundamentals for B2B product and sales teams
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: SaaStr / Jason Lemkin
items.body:
## Why it is worth taking

SaaStr's courses provide practical, battle-tested advice from Jason Lemkin and other B2B SaaS veterans. The enterprise sales course covers: how to build an enterprise sales team, how to price enterprise deals, how to handle POCs, and how to avoid common enterprise pitfalls.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers who work closely with enterprise sales

## Key takeaway

Enterprise sales requires a different playbook than SMB. Longer cycles, more stakeholders, and higher expectations. The course provides a structured playbook for navigating enterprise deals.

items.title: The Secrets of B2B Product Management (LinkedIn Learning)
items.summary: LinkedIn Learning course covering the fundamentals of B2B product management including stakeholder analysis and roadmap communication
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Leah Tharin / LinkedIn Learning
items.body:
## Why it is worth taking

This course by Leah Tharin provides a comprehensive introduction to B2B product management. It covers: the key differences between B2B and B2C product management, how to work with enterprise stakeholders, how to build a B2B roadmap, and how to run discovery in B2B contexts.

## Best for

New or aspiring B2B Product Managers, or B2C PMs transitioning to B2B

## Key takeaway

The course provides a solid foundation in B2B PM fundamentals with practical frameworks and templates you can apply immediately. Short modules make it easy to fit into a busy schedule.

items.title: The B2B Product Manager's Dilemma: Balancing Revenue and Vision
items.summary: Analysis of how B2B PMs navigate the tension between short-term revenue-driven requests and long-term product vision
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Leah Tharin
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

This article articulates a tension every B2B PM faces: the sales team wants specific features to close deals, but those requests may not align with the product vision. Leah Tharin provides a framework for navigating this tension without alienating sales or abandoning strategy.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers struggling with sales-driven feature requests

## Key takeaway

Create a structured process for evaluating revenue-driven requests: does this feature unlock new segments, increase ACV, or prevent churn? If yes, it belongs on the roadmap alongside vision-driven work.

items.title: B2B Customer Onboarding: The First 90 Days
items.summary: Research-backed guide to designing effective B2B customer onboarding programs that reduce time-to-value and churn
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Gainsight / Pulse Blog
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

This article (from Gainsight's customer success expertise) covers how to design a B2B onboarding program that gets customers to value quickly. It covers: pre-onboarding preparation, Day 1 activities, the 30-60-90 day framework, and success criteria at each milestone.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers looking to improve activation rates

## Key takeaway

B2B onboarding should be milestone-based, not time-based. Define what 'value' looks like for each customer segment and build onboarding steps that lead directly to that value — not generic feature walkthroughs.

items.title: The B2B PLG Playbook: From Signup to Enterprise Deal
items.summary: Step-by-step guide on building a hybrid product-led and sales-led growth motion for B2B SaaS
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Kyle Poyar / OpenView
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Kyle Poyar's article provides a detailed playbook for combining product-led and sales-led growth in B2B. It covers: when to add a sales team to a PLG motion, how to define product-qualified leads (PQLs), and how to hand off from product to sales without friction.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers at PLG-first startups adding enterprise sales motion

## Key takeaway

The handoff from self-serve to sales is critical. Define clear PQL criteria (usage milestones, team size, feature adoption) so sales only touches leads that are ready for a conversation. Don't let sales interrupt self-serve users.

items.title: How to Run Effective B2B Product Discovery
items.summary: Practical guide to adapting product discovery for B2B contexts with limited customer access
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Teresa Torres / Product Talk
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Teresa Torres's blog is a treasure trove of practical discovery advice. This article specifically addresses B2B challenges: few customers, long sales cycles, and multiple stakeholders. She covers how to get access to customers, what to ask, and how to synthesise findings.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers who want a systematic discovery practice

## Key takeaway

Run opportunity solution trees to map your thinking, interview customers weekly (even 15 minutes), and focus on recent, specific behaviour — not opinions or hypotheticals.

items.title: B2B SaaS Pricing: Value Metrics that Scale
items.summary: How to choose value metrics for B2B pricing that grow with customer success
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Patrick Campbell / ProfitWell (Paddle)
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

This article by Patrick Campbell (ProfitWell) explains how to choose a value metric for B2B SaaS pricing — the unit that determines how much a customer pays. Examples: per seat, per API call, per document processed, per workflow. The right value metric aligns your revenue with the value customers receive.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers designing or revising pricing models

## Key takeaway

The best value metrics are: aligned with the value customers perceive, able to grow with the customer (no artificial ceilings), and simple to understand and communicate. Avoid per-seat pricing if the value doesn't scale with user count.

items.title: Product Thinking in B2B vs B2C
items.summary: Comparison of product management approaches in B2B and B2C contexts highlighting key differences
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Marty Cagan / SVPG Blog
items.body:
## Why it is worth reading

Marty Cagan contrasts B2B and B2C product management. Key B2B differences: longer sales cycles, multiple buyer personas per account, higher switching costs, the need for sales and support alignment, and the importance of customer success.

## Best for

B2C PMs transitioning to B2B or B2B PMs looking to validate their approach

## Key takeaway

B2B product management is not harder or easier than B2C — it's different. The core principles (outcome over output, empowered teams, continuous discovery) apply in both contexts, but the tactics differ significantly.

items.title: B2B Product-Led Growth (by Wes Bush)
items.summary: Wes Bush's podcast dedicated to B2B product-led growth strategies, case studies, and interviews with PLG leaders
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Wes Bush / ProductLed
items.body:
## Why it is worth subscribing to

Wes Bush hosts practical, interview-based episodes with B2B founders and product leaders who have successfully implemented PLG. Topics include: building virality into B2B products, freemium vs free trial decisions, and product-qualified lead strategies.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers implementing or refining PLG strategies

## Key takeaway

Each episode includes actionable takeaways you can apply to your product. The case studies cover companies at different stages, from early-stage startups to enterprise-scale PLG.

items.title: SaaStr Podcast
items.summary: Jason Lemkin's long-running podcast interviewing B2B SaaS founders, CEOs, and product leaders about growth and strategy
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: SaaStr / Jason Lemkin
items.body:
## Why it is worth subscribing to

The SaaStr Podcast features candid interviews with B2B SaaS founders and executives. Episodes cover: fundraising, scaling sales, product strategy, and building culture. The 'Office Hours' format allows listeners to submit questions.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers who want to understand the business side of their product decisions

## Key takeaway

Jason Lemkin's straight-talking style provides unfiltered insights into what works (and doesn't) in B2B SaaS. The podcast covers the full business lifecycle from seed to IPO.

items.title: Product Coalition Podcast
items.summary: Product management podcast with regular B2B-focused episodes on stakeholder management, roadmapping, and product discovery
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Product Coalition
items.body:
## Why it is worth subscribing to

The Product Coalition podcast interviews product leaders from top companies. Many episodes focus on B2B product management: how to manage enterprise stakeholders, how to build B2B roadmaps, and how to run discovery with corporate customers.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers looking for practical, experience-based advice

## Key takeaway

The podcast brings diverse perspectives from PMs at different companies and stages. The B2B-specific episodes provide frameworks you can adapt to your context.

items.title: Product Thinking (by Product School)
items.summary: Product School's podcast covering product strategy, growth, and innovation with frequent B2B SaaS product deep dives
items.author: MILO Team
items.creator: Product School
items.body:
## Why it is worth subscribing to

Hosted by Carlos Gonzalez de Villaumbrosia (Product School CEO), this podcast interviews product leaders from companies like Salesforce, Slack, and HubSpot. Episodes cover B2B-specific challenges and product management career development.

## Best for

B2B Product Managers at all levels who want to learn from experienced leaders

## Key takeaway

The podcast offers both tactical advice (how to run a B2B discovery interview) and strategic perspectives (how to build a product org for enterprise).

items.title: Masters of Scale with Reid Hoffman
